summary.text: Jon Ossoff is the incumbent Democratic U.S. Senator from Georgia, first elected in a January 2021 runoff. A former congressional aide and head of an investigative-documentary company, he lost a 2017 special election for the U.S. House before winning the Senate seat. He is running for re-election on his Senate record, including prescription-drug costs, fentanyl detection and corruption investigations.

paragraphs.text: Ossoff was born on February 16, 1987, in Atlanta, and his Senate website describes him as born and raised in Georgia.
He earned a bachelor's degree from Georgetown University's School of Foreign Service in 2009 and a master's degree from the London School of Economics in 2013.

From 2007 to 2012 he worked as a national security and foreign affairs legislative staffer for U.S. Rep. Hank Johnson of Georgia, according to Wikipedia, handling defense and economic policy, and his Senate website says he was mentored by Rep. John Lewis.

Ossoff has been managing director and CEO of the filmmaking company Insight TWI since 2013; his Senate website says the company produced investigative journalism on war crimes, public corruption, human trafficking and organized crime.

Ossoff ran in the 2017 special election for Georgia's 6th Congressional District, finishing first in the April primary and losing the June 20 runoff to Republican Karen Handel, 48.2% to 51.8%; he did not run for the seat in 2018.

In 2020 he won the June 9 Democratic primary for U.S. Senate with 52.8% of the vote, then defeated incumbent Sen. David Perdue (R) in the January 5, 2021, general runoff, 50.6% to 49.4%; he assumed office on January 20, 2021.

In the 2025-2026 Congress Ossoff sits on the Appropriations Committee, where he is ranking member of the Military Construction, Veterans Affairs subcommittee, and on the Rules and Administration Committee and the Select Committee on Intelligence.

His Senate website cites bipartisan legislation on online child safety, veterans' mental health care and fentanyl trafficking, along with investigations of federal prisons and privatized military housing, and says he passed more standalone bills in his first two years in office than any other freshman senator.
He lives in Atlanta with his wife, Dr. Alisha Kramer, and their two daughters.
